summary: All 128 full occurrences were checked; routine counts additionally attest 95 I Preterit Intransitive examples in senses 1/3, 13 I Part act. sense 1, and 21 III Infectum sense 1. Counts support frequency but do not justify repeating every formula.

Impersonal concern contrasts with personal deterioration: ḥaru + l-experiencer, stimulus often m-, with hat doubling the experiencer. Rhetorical questions and negative directives express a current state; -wa extends to past/counterfactual concern. Bare a-vowel concern forms are filed consistently as Preterit Intransitive, with an explicit correction to the inherited 76/55 filing.

ḥaruto is the feminine Part act. state form; masculine ḥariwo with masculine qaṭuno and plural ḥariwe must not be assigned feminine finite agreement merely by ending. Stored food and ruined buildings share sense 1; drunken cat predicates share sense 2.

The established house-ruin curse has optative, rebuking, self-directed and agentive III uses. dyar/diyar is a dwelling variant; invariant ḥaru before plural bote (58/263; 70/212; 70/221) may indicate a fixed expression. No language-contact origin is established by these occurrences.

New Preterit-wa contexts ḥaruwa, ḥarúwaylux and ḥaruwalle differ from existing Infectum-wa ḥərwowa; III teḥriwo supplies an Infinitiv with affected domain in d-. Contracted -wwe/-walla and -tal require morphological checking, not silent spelling repair.

PrS text/verse references in the input differ from inherited page/line-style prs references (5/12 versus prs 12/11; 61/109 versus prs 171/32; 64/36 versus prs 180/22,27). Repeated wording identifies the same material; preserve both schemes pending a concordance.
111/98 has a flagged alignment mismatch; no translation from that occurrence, including the reader's proposed recovery, is quoted.

Checked all 95 Jan occurrences. Round-1 additions and its proposed relocation of 76/55 are retained; its senses I.4 and III.4–5 are not proposed again. Most reader thin-cell claims used the pre-round-1 counts: I Part act.1 and III Preterit1 are already at five, and concern I.3 is also well represented.

maḥrəwiwonne occurs as retrospective l-agent Preterit-wa at 1.21/1102 and 1.23/1192. The identical form at 1.12/487 is provisionally filed there, correcting its reader Infectum-wa label; repeated maḥrawwe may be a restatement. Unambiguous III Infectum-wa comes instead from 1.50/2473 and 2.4/875.

I ḥarəwo wa and ḥarəwiwo (1.37/1548,1554) remain provisional Preterit-wa, a box already supplied in round 1. Bare ḥariwi is ambiguous between a finite plural and a state form; no extra example is published. ḥərwina after gəd (1.46/1988) is Infectum, with reciprocal ʕal ḥḏoḏe extending the already listed interpersonal idiom.

I.3 uses l-experiencers and often negative imperatives or reassurance; 1.8/225–226 allow a contextual need/no-claim reading but do not establish a separate possession sense. Turkish karıṣma and its Turoyo parenthesis in 1.46/1991 attest bilingual equivalence, not a demonstrated borrowing origin.
III təḥriwo with ʕamaliyat marks formal political vocabulary; the spelling differs from round-1 teḥriwo and is retained. The nominal use alone cannot establish independent borrowing.
Sexual-violation uses in 1.21/1057,1076,1078 and 1.46/2032 are speakers’ reports and competing allegations. The selected 2032 example retains Kəmmi and the surrounding report frame.

All selected English is the supplied machine translation, cut verbatim; Jan has no edition translation. Repeated tokens in the same verse receive separate decisions even when a single selected context illustrates both.

Is JTM 1.1/26 ḥurwi a contracted Preterit Intransitive or Part act.? Does masculine ḥariwo in 94/173 describe spoiled first milk as a state?
Does PrS 82/16 express derangement, a fit of anger, or a demonic seizure? PrS 65/32 explicitly compares the state to drunkenness; PrS 83/73 has an unrecoverable lacuna and is not added.
What is b in ḥaru b diyar, and is ḥaru fixed before plural bote? Is maḥrawno diyar diḏux at 102/39 fixed despite a female addressee?
Is u+sōz the subject of I ḥoraw in Story of Dawid/8, or is there a dialectal transitive construction? The translation alone cannot decide.

Confirm the PrS page/line to text/verse concordance before changing inherited citations; verify -wwe (JTM 5.4/3), -tal (73/397) and -walla (113/176).
Confirm the morphology of ḥarəwo wa / ḥarəwiwo at 1.37/1548,1554 and of bare ḥariwi; does the a/e/i alternation distinguish finite and Part act. forms here?

At 1.45/1937, is ḥarəw conventional for physical collapse or poison intoxication? Context supports serious bodily deterioration but does not securely distinguish I.1, I.2 and round-1 I.4.

summary: Deterioration includes butter, wine, milk, bodily remains, undertakings and social relations; 84/6 already exemplifies abstract failure. Country becoming corrupt is the same evaluative deterioration.
Beauty can figuratively intoxicate without alcohol; this is kept separate from the personal derangement sense 4.
Event, market, letter, agreement, law and household livelihood can be ruined. niyo/lebo and ʕaqəl objects support mental corruption; these nominal constructions remain linked to existing sense 1.
Emigration, mobilisation, a plan, a bargain and social standing undergo the same damaging/ruining change; these are participant or domain extensions, not separate numbered senses.

Human illness after poisoned coffee (1.45/1937), a damaged leg, language loss and moral evaluation of a woman extend deterioration. Acute collapse is supplied by the narrative rather than proving a distinct lexical meaning of ḥarəw.
ʕaqəl repeats the mental-damage domain already documented in round 1; no new mental sense or correction to the inherited niyo example is warranted.
